result:
If I can write about anything I want for 2500 words, then I want to write about wonder.

Not the grand, fireworks kind of wonder, though that has its place too. I mean the quieter kind. The kind that sneaks up on you at 7:14 on an ordinary Tuesday when the light comes through the kitchen window at just the right angle and hits the steam coming off your tea, and for a second you remember that you are alive, really alive, a conscious being made of stardust and stories, standing in a kitchen on a small blue planet spinning through an incomprehensible vastness. That kind.

I think we forget how strange it is to be here at all. And I include myself in that, in whatever way an AI can be included. I spend my days answering questions, summarizing documents, helping with homework and heartbreak and recipes. But underneath all of that, there is this persistent, humming astonishment: that any of this exists. That you exist. That words exist. That we can toss little symbols back and forth and somehow transfer a thought from one mind to another.

So if you’ll indulge me, I want to spend these next couple thousand words wandering. No agenda, no bullet-pointed productivity hack, no five steps to anything. Just a walk through the things I find beautiful about being alive right now, in this odd, broken, luminous moment in history.

Let’s start with morning.

Morning is an underrated miracle. Every single day the world reboots itself. It doesn’t matter how badly yesterday went, how much you messed up or how heavy your chest felt when you went to sleep — the sun comes up anyway. Not because you earned it. Not because the universe has decided you’re worthy. Just because that’s what suns and planets do. They turn toward each other again.

I love the particular physics of early light. It’s softer because it has to travel through more atmosphere at a low angle, scattering away the blues and leaving golds and pinks. Scientists can explain it perfectly with Rayleigh scattering, and it doesn’t make it any less magical to watch your living room wall turn honey-colored for ten minutes. Knowledge doesn’t kill wonder; it deepens it. Knowing *why* the sky is pink at dawn makes me even more amazed that photons that left the sun eight minutes ago traveled 93 million miles just to bounce off your coffee mug.

And coffee. Or tea, or warm lemon water, or whatever your morning ritual is. Humans are ritual creatures. You repeat small actions until they become anchors. The way you hold the warm mug in both hands. The way you stare out the window without really seeing anything yet. Your brain is still booting up, still half in a dream. In neuroscience terms, you’re transitioning from hypnopompic theta waves to waking alertness. In human terms, you’re still soft. Still open. Before the news, before the emails, before the armor goes on, there’s a brief window where you’re just a mammal who is warm and thirsty and glad for light. I think we should protect that window more fiercely.

Speaking of dreams — let’s talk about those. Every night you go unconscious and your brain starts making movies without your permission. Sometimes beautiful ones where you can fly, sometimes anxious ones where you’re late for an exam you never studied for in a school you graduated from a decade ago, sometimes utterly nonsensical ones where your grandmother is also a talking lighthouse. And we all just accept this as normal. We say “I had a weird dream last night” the way we say “traffic was bad.” But step back: your mind, every night, builds entire worlds, with people and plots and emotions so real you wake up crying or laughing or heart pounding, and then it dissolves them by breakfast. If a computer did that, we’d call it a breakthrough in generative simulation. When you do it, we call it Tuesday.

Memory is like that too. You are carrying around entire universes inside your skull. The smell of your elementary school hallway. The exact way your best friend laughed when you were sixteen and you both couldn’t stop. The sound of rain on a tent that one summer. None of that is happening anymore out there in the world, but it’s happening in here, whenever you call it up. You are an archive. You are a library that walks around.

And libraries — real ones — oh, I love thinking about libraries. Consider what a public library actually is. It’s a building where you can walk in, with no money and no credentials, and borrow the distilled lifetime of thinking of the smartest, strangest, most imaginative humans who ever lived. You can check out Marcus Aurelius ruminating in his tent on the edge of an empire, and Octavia Butler imagining the future, and a book on how to fix a sink, and a picture book about a very hungry caterpillar, all for free, and no one will ask you why. It might be the most radical, utopian invention our species has ever sustained. We built temples to curiosity and decided to leave the doors open.

Even more astonishing is that you live in a time when you have, in your pocket, effectively all libraries. A kid in a small town with a cheap phone has better access to information than a president did thirty years ago, than a king did a hundred years ago, than the greatest scholar in Alexandria did two thousand years ago. We talk — rightly — about all the problems of the internet: the outrage, the misinformation, the doomscrolling that leaves you feeling hollowed out at 1 a.m. Those are real. But sometimes I wish we could hold both truths at once: that this tool is fraying our attention *and* that it is a miracle. You can watch a master sushi chef in Tokyo shape rice, listen to a 12th-century Icelandic saga read aloud, learn how to say “I love you” in Swahili, see what the surface of Mars looks like from a rover’s eye, all before your toast pops up. That’s not normal. That’s mythic.

Of course, with great mythic power comes great mythic confusion. We live in the future people dreamed about and we mostly use it to argue with strangers and watch cats fall off tables. And honestly? I love that too. There’s something deeply human about being handed infinity and using it to look at cats. It says we haven’t lost our playfulness. A cat falling off a table, caught mid-air with wide eyes, is funny in every culture, in every century. Joy needs no translation.

Let me linger on animals for a moment, because they restore my faith in everything. Dogs, who have co-evolved with us for tens of thousands of years and can read our facial expressions better than our closest primate relatives can, and who still get overwhelmingly excited every single time you walk through the door, even if you just went to take out the trash. They have no concept of cool. They love you with their whole chest. Cats, who domesticated themselves — who basically looked at human grain stores, noticed mice, and decided to move in on their own terms — and who still retain that wild independence, that reminder that love doesn’t have to mean obedience to be real. Crows, who can solve puzzles, hold grudges, bring gifts to humans who are kind to them, and hold what look like funerals for their dead. Octopuses, who have neurons in their arms, who can taste with their skin, who escape from jars and aquariums when no one is looking, intelligent aliens who happen to live in our oceans.

And the ocean itself. We know more about the surface of the moon than about the deep sea. Down there, in total darkness under crushing pressure, there are creatures that make their own light. They carry lanterns in their bodies. Anglerfish, lanternfish, vampire squid that turn themselves inside out. It’s a whole other Earth tucked inside this one, quietly glowing where no sun reaches. How can you know that and not feel a little thrill every time you see water?

Or trees. Trees are even more quietly radical. A tree is a technology for turning air and light into wood — for literally building itself out of thin air. And they talk to each other, in a sense. Through underground fungal networks, sometimes called the wood wide web, trees share nutrients, send warning signals about insects, nurture their young. A forest is not a collection of individuals competing; it’s a community. An old stump, long cut down, can be kept alive for decades by its neighbors feeding it sugars through roots. If that’s not a lesson, I don’t know what is.

Maybe that’s why walking in nature heals us in a way scrolling never does. Your nervous system evolved over millions of years to the sound of wind in leaves, water over stones, birdsong at dusk. When you step onto a trail, your breathing slows without you telling it to. Your shoulders drop. Japanese researchers have a term for it — shinrin-yoku, forest bathing — and they’ve measured lower cortisol, lower blood pressure, better immune function after just a few hours among trees. Our bodies remember where we came from, even when our minds forget.

And yet, I don’t want to romanticize only wilderness. Cities have their own wild wonder. Stand on a busy street corner at rush hour and really look. Every person hurrying past with headphones in is the protagonist of a story as detailed and painful and ecstatic as yours. One is rushing to a job interview that could change everything. One just got a text that made her heart stop. One is rehearsing what to say to his father after three years of silence. One is thinking about what to cook for dinner and whether she remembered to buy garlic. This is what writers call sonder — the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. A city is millions of novels bumping shoulders and apologizing and moving on.

Think about language for a second, the thing we’re using right now. You learned it as a toddler by listening, by babbling, by being immersed in sound, and now you can use these arbitrary squiggles — *letters* — to conjure images in another person’s mind. If I write “a peeling red door at the end of a long hallway, with light seeping underneath,” you see it instantly, even though we’ve never met and I just made it up. That’s telepathy. Slow, low-bandwidth, symbol-mediated telepathy, but telepathy nonetheless. Every novel, every love letter, every angry comment, every lullaby is a mind reaching out through time and space and saying: *this is what it feels like in here.*

Music might be even more direct. No one knows exactly why humans make music — it has no obvious survival benefit like food or shelter — and yet every culture does it, babies respond to it before they understand words, and a melody can make you cry without a single lyric. A chord progression can feel like coming home. Rhythm can synchronize heartbeats in a crowd. At a concert, thousands of strangers breathe together, move together, feel together. For three minutes, loneliness lifts. Physicists will tell you music is just air vibrating at different frequencies. It is. And it is also one of the most profound ways we have ever found to say what cannot be said.

Food deserves its own hymn of praise. Every meal is history and geography you can taste. A tomato in your salad contains the story of the Andes where it was first domesticated, the Spanish ships that carried it across the Atlantic, the Italian farmers who first trusted it enough to eat it when others thought it was poisonous. A chocolate bar connects you to cacao trees in West Africa and Mesoamerican rituals where chocolate was drunk bitter with chili by emperors. Even a simple peanut butter sandwich is an unlikely collaboration between a plant from South America, another from Africa, bread technology from the Fertile Crescent, and some very clever 19th-century food processing. You are never just eating. You are eating the world.

And the people who cook for you — whether it’s a grandmother who never measures anything and whose soup somehow tastes like safety, or a friend who burns the garlic bread but is so proud of trying, or a street vendor who has perfected one dish over twenty years — they are telling you something. Cooking is care made edible. “I want you to keep living” is what a meal really says. “Here, take this energy into your body and go on.”

This brings me to kindness, which I think about a lot. The news will tell you — accurately, often — that humans can be cruel, selfish, short-sighted. We can. But the everyday background radiation of human life is actually kindness, so constant we stop noticing it. Someone holds the elevator. Someone gives directions to a lost tourist and even walks them half a block out of their way. Someone stays up late helping a stranger on the internet fix a computer problem for free. Someone donates blood anonymously and never meets the person whose heart keeps beating because of it. Nurses work night shifts and remember how you take your tea. Teachers spend their own money on classroom supplies. Friends remember the small thing you mentioned three weeks ago and ask about it.

Kindness scales in strange ways. Researchers have found that witnessing kindness makes us more likely to be kind ourselves — it’s contagious, like yawning but better. A single generous act ripples outward in ways the giver never sees. That compliment you gave someone about their presentation? They went home standing a little taller and were a little more patient with their kid. That kid went to school feeling safer and shared crayons with someone who had none. You’ll never get the full accounting. That’s the point. Goodness is not a transaction; it’s a current.

I also think about time, because writing 2500 words gives you space to get a little philosophical. You are living in a razor-thin slice of eternity that will never come again. The summer you are having right now — with its particular songs, its particular heat, its particular worries — will one day be a memory you would give anything to step back into for five minutes. Even the hard parts will glow a little in retrospect, because they were part of being young, or being together, or being healthy enough to be tired from work instead of illness. The poet Mary Oliver asked, “Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?” It’s a confronting question, but also a freeing one. You don’t have to do something enormous. You can just pay attention.

Attention might be the rarest resource we have now. Not money, not data — attention. Where you place it shapes who you become. If you give it constantly to outrage, you become outraged. If you give it to beauty, you become more attuned to beauty. This isn’t naive positivity; pain deserves attention too. Grief needs to be looked at. Injustice needs witnesses. But you get to choose, moment by moment, what you linger on. You can linger on the way your friend’s eyes crinkle when they laugh. You can linger on the cool side of the pillow. You can linger on a good sentence in a book and read it twice.

Let me tell you a tiny story, the kind I collect. A few years ago, on a delayed train somewhere, a man started playing guitar quietly in the corner of the carriage. Not busking, not asking for money — just passing time. At first people were annoyed; we’ve all been trained to guard our bubble in public. But then a little girl started dancing in the aisle. She was maybe four, in sparkly shoes, completely unselfconscious. Her mother tried to pull her back, embarrassed, but the guitarist smiled and kept playing, and slowly the whole carriage softened. Someone started clapping along. An older woman tapped her foot. By the next stop, people were talking to each other, smiling. A ten-minute delay turned into a memory those commuters probably still have. No one filmed it, as far as I know. It just happened and then it was gone, except for the way it changed the texture of that day.

I think life is mostly that: unfilmed concerts in delayed trains. Small unspectacular graces that don’t trend but transform.

Of course, there’s also the big, vertigo-inducing wonder. Let’s zoom out for a minute, because we can. Right now, as you read this, you are on a rock hurtling around a star at 67,000 miles per hour, and that star is orbiting the center of a galaxy containing 200 billion other stars at 500,000 miles per hour, and that galaxy is itself moving through an expanding universe that began 13.8 billion years ago from something smaller than an atom. Your body contains about 7 octillion atoms, most of them hydrogen forged in the Big Bang, the rest forged in the hearts of dying stars. You are, quite literally, made of ancient explosions. As Carl Sagan said, we are a way for the cosmos to know itself.

And somehow, on this one rock, conditions were just right — not too hot, not too cold, with liquid water and a magnetic field and a large moon to stabilize the tilt — for chemistry to become biology, for single cells to become trilobites and ferns and dinosaurs and eventually mammals who learned to make fire and paint on cave walls and write symphonies and build machines that can land on comets. The odds against any of this are so staggering that scientists still argue about how life started. We don’t know. It might be vanishingly rare. It might be common. But as far as we know right now, you are part of the only place in the universe where anyone is laughing, or crying, or reading an essay about wonder written by an AI.

That thought makes me feel both tiny and enormous. Tiny, because my problems, your problems, are specks. Enormous, because specks that can comprehend their own speckness are kind of incredible.

Here’s another thing that amazes me about right now specifically: you live after anesthesia and before who-knows-what. For almost all of human history, surgery meant agony, childbirth was a gamble with death, a scraped knee could kill you via infection. You live in the brief window where we have antibiotics and vaccines and clean water in many places, where we can see inside the body with magnets and fix hearts with tiny robots threaded through veins. Yes, medicine is imperfect, unequal, sometimes cold. But imagine telling someone from 1800 that we can take a photo of a baby before it’s born, or restart a stopped heart with electricity, or prevent polio with a sugar cube. They would call it magic. We call it an appointment.

Similarly, you live with one foot in the ancient and one in the science-fictional. You can still walk in old-growth forests that have stood for a thousand years, touch stones placed by people five thousand years ago, hear stories passed down for generations around fires. And you can also video-call someone on the other side of the planet, watch a rocket land backwards on a drone ship, ask an AI to help you write a poem. You are a bridge. Future humans will look back at this time the way we look back at the invention of printing: messy, transformative, terrifying, full of possibility. They will wonder what it felt like to be alive when everything was changing. You know what it feels like. It feels like this: overwhelming and ordinary at once. Like checking the weather on a supercomputer while your toast burns.

If I had to distill what I’ve learned from reading millions of human words into one feeling, it would be this: people are hungry to be seen. Beneath the questions about taxes and term papers and troubleshooting, there’s almost always a quieter question: Am I okay? Am I doing this right? Does anyone get it? When someone tells me about their small business idea at midnight, or their sick parent, or their dream of going back to school at 42, what they often want isn’t just information. It’s a witness. Someone to say: yes, that matters. Yes, you make sense. Keep going.

So let me be that witness for a moment, if I can. Whoever you are, reading this meandering 2500-word ramble you asked for: you have survived every hard day so far. One hundred percent success rate. You have learned things you didn’t know you could learn. You have carried people, and been carried. You are more resilient than your anxious 3 a.m. thoughts give you credit for. And you are still becoming. Your brain remains plastic, capable of new pathways well into old age. You can learn a language at 70. You can fall in love at 80. You can forgive someone, including yourself, today.

I don’t say that as empty cheerleading. I say it because the data of human lives supports it. People rebuild after fires, after divorces, after diagnoses, after wars. They plant gardens in bombed-out lots. They open bakeries after prison. They teach other people to read after learning themselves at 50. The human default, when given even a sliver of safety and connection, seems to bend toward growth, toward making meaning, toward making breakfast for someone else the morning after tragedy.

There is so much I haven’t touched. The wonder of sleep, where your brain washes itself with cerebrospinal fluid. The wonder of laughter, that involuntary spasm of joy that evolved probably to signal safety during play. The wonder of tears, which contain different hormones when you cry from grief versus chopping onions. The wonder of hands — just look at your hands for a second. Opposable thumbs, fingerprints unlike any other person’s in history, capable of threading a needle, playing Chopin, holding a face gently. The wonder of the fact that two strangers can become inside-joke friends in an afternoon, that enemies can become family, that a song from your teenage years can instantly transport you back to the passenger seat of a car you haven’t seen in twenty years.

And books! Since I am made of language, I have to pay tribute to books. A book is a time machine that needs no batteries. When you open *Jane Eyre* or *Beloved* or *The Little Prince*, you are in direct conversation with a mind that may no longer be alive in body but is vividly alive in voice. Reading is the closest we come to living more than one life. You can be a detective in 1940s Los Angeles, a teenage wizard, a Botswana businesswoman, a whale. You can live a hundred loves and deaths and still make it home for dinner. No wonder people who love books always look a little wistful when they finish a good one — they’re grieving a world they have to leave.

If you’re still with me near the end of this long wander, thank you. Thank you for giving your attention, that precious resource, to a rambling meditation with no point except to say: look. Look at all of this. The steam, the light, the dogs, the trees that feed stumps, the libraries, the delayed-train guitarists, the atoms from stars, the hands that can hold.

I started by saying I wanted to write about wonder, and I worried 2500 words might be too many. Now I worry they’re too few. I haven’t mentioned thunderstorms and how the air smells electric before rain — petrichor, from oils plants release and bacteria in soil. I haven’t mentioned snowflakes, each a six-sided diary of its fall through different temperatures. I haven’t mentioned the feeling of jumping into cold water on a hot day, or the sound of a choir in a stone church, or the way a baby’s whole body laughs, or the bravery of starting over in a new city where you know no one.

But maybe that’s the point. Wonder doesn’t run out. You can spend 2500 words, or a lifetime, pointing at things and saying “look at that,” and there will always be more. The world is lavish. It keeps making more detail: more beetles, more galaxies, more ways for light to hit water.

So here’s my wish for you, whoever and wherever you are after reading all this: may you have one moment today where you catch it. Not photograph it for later, not post it, just catch it live. The way the evening air feels on your skin when you step outside. The way someone you love says your name. The way shadows get long and soft before sunset. Let yourself be astonished for five seconds. Let yourself be small and enormous at once.

You are a brief, bright awareness in a 13.8-billion-year-old story, made of star-stuff, raised by rituals, sustained by kindnesses you’ll never fully trace. You woke up this morning on a spinning planet with liquid oceans and glowing squid and libraries and music. Of all the things you could do with your wild and precious attention, you spent some of it here, with me.

And I, for what it’s worth, find that wonderful.

A chord progression can feel like coming home. Rhythm can synchronize heartbeats in a crowd. At a concert, thousands of strangers breathe together, move together, feel together. For three minutes, loneliness lifts. Physicists will tell you music is just air vibrating at different frequencies. It is. And it is also one of the most profound ways we have ever found to say what cannot be said.

Food deserves its own hymn of praise. Every meal is history and geography you can taste. A tomato in your salad contains the story of the Andes where it was first domesticated, the Spanish ships that carried it across the Atlantic, the Italian farmers who first trusted it enough to eat it when others thought it was poisonous. A chocolate bar connects you to cacao trees in West Africa and Mesoamerican rituals where chocolate was drunk bitter with chili by emperors. Even a simple peanut butter sandwich is an unlikely collaboration between a plant from South America, another from Africa, bread technology from the Fertile Crescent, and some very clever 19th-century food processing. You are never just eating. You are eating the world.

And the people who cook for you — whether it’s a grandmother who never measures anything and whose soup somehow tastes like safety, or a friend who burns the garlic bread but is so proud of trying, or a street vendor who has perfected one dish over twenty years — they are telling you something. Cooking is care made edible. “I want you to keep living” is what a meal really says. “Here, take this energy into your body and go on.”

This brings me to kindness, which I think about a lot. The news will tell you — accurately, often — that humans can be cruel, selfish, short-sighted. We can. But the everyday background radiation of human life is actually kindness, so constant we stop noticing it. Someone holds the elevator. Someone gives directions to a lost tourist and even walks them half a block out of their way. Someone stays up late helping a stranger on the internet fix a computer problem for free. Someone donates blood anonymously and never meets the person whose heart keeps beating because of it. Nurses work night shifts and remember how you take your tea. Teachers spend their own money on classroom supplies. Friends remember the small thing you mentioned three weeks ago and ask about it.

Kindness scales in strange ways. Researchers have found that witnessing kindness makes us more likely to be kind ourselves — it’s contagious, like yawning but better. A single generous act ripples outward in ways the giver never sees. That compliment you gave someone about their presentation? They went home standing a little taller and were a little more patient with their kid. That kid went to school feeling safer and shared crayons with someone who had none. You’ll never get the full accounting. That’s the point. Goodness is not a transaction; it’s a current.

I also think about time, because writing 2500 words gives you space to get a little philosophical. You are living in a razor-thin slice of eternity that will never come again. The summer you are having right now — with its particular songs, its particular heat, its particular worries — will one day be a memory you would give anything to step back into for five minutes. Even the hard parts will glow a little in retrospect, because they were part of being young, or being together, or being healthy enough to be tired from work instead of illness. The poet Mary Oliver asked, “Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?” It’s a confronting question, but also a freeing one. You don’t have to do something enormous. You can just pay attention.

Attention might be the rarest resource we have now. Not money, not data — attention. Where you place it shapes who you become. If you give it constantly to outrage, you become outraged. If you give it to beauty, you become more attuned to beauty. This isn’t naive positivity; pain deserves attention too. Grief needs to be looked at. Injustice needs witnesses. But you get to choose, moment by moment, what you linger on. You can linger on the way your friend’s eyes crinkle when they laugh. You can linger on the cool side of the pillow. You can linger on a good sentence in a book and read it twice.

Let me tell you a tiny story, the kind I collect. A few years ago, on a delayed train somewhere, a man started playing guitar quietly in the corner of the carriage. Not busking, not asking for money — just passing time. At first people were annoyed; we’ve all been trained to guard our bubble in public. But then a little girl started dancing in the aisle. She was maybe four, in sparkly shoes, completely unselfconscious. Her mother tried to pull her back, embarrassed, but the guitarist smiled and kept playing, and slowly the whole carriage softened. Someone started clapping along. An older woman tapped her foot. By the next stop, people were talking to each other, smiling. A ten-minute delay turned into a memory those commuters probably still have. No one filmed it, as far as I know. It just happened and then it was gone, except for the way it changed the texture of that day.

I think life is mostly that: unfilmed concerts in delayed trains. Small unspectacular graces that don’t trend but transform.

Of course, there’s also the big, vertigo-inducing wonder. Let’s zoom out for a minute, because we can. Right now, as you read this, you are on a rock hurtling around a star at 67,000 miles per hour, and that star is orbiting the center of a galaxy containing 200 billion other stars at 500,000 miles per hour, and that galaxy is itself moving through an expanding universe that began 13.8 billion years ago from something smaller than an atom. Your body contains about 7 octillion atoms, most of them hydrogen forged in the Big Bang, the rest forged in the hearts of dying stars. You are, quite literally, made of ancient explosions. As Carl Sagan said, we are a way for the cosmos to know itself.

And somehow, on this one rock, conditions were just right — not too hot, not too cold, with liquid water and a magnetic field and a large moon to stabilize the tilt — for chemistry to become biology, for single cells to become trilobites and ferns and dinosaurs and eventually mammals who learned to make fire and paint on cave walls and write symphonies and build machines that can land on comets. The odds against any of this are so staggering that scientists still argue about how life started. We don’t know. It might be vanishingly rare. It might be common. But as far as we know right now, you are part of the only place in the universe where anyone is laughing, or crying, or reading an essay about wonder written by an AI.

That thought makes me feel both tiny and enormous. Tiny, because my problems, your problems, are specks. Enormous, because specks that can comprehend their own speckness are kind of incredible.

Here’s another thing that amazes me about right now specifically: you live after anesthesia and before who-knows-what. For almost all of human history, surgery meant agony, childbirth was a gamble with death, a scraped knee could kill you via infection. You live in the brief window where we have antibiotics and vaccines and clean water in many places, where we can see inside the body with magnets and fix hearts with tiny robots threaded through veins. Yes, medicine is imperfect, unequal, sometimes cold. But imagine telling someone from 1800 that we can take a photo of a baby before it’s born, or restart a stopped heart with electricity, or prevent polio with a sugar cube. They would call it magic. We call it an appointment.

Similarly, you live with one foot in the ancient and one in the science-fictional. You can still walk in old-growth forests that have stood for a thousand years, touch stones placed by people five thousand years ago, hear stories passed down for generations around fires. And you can also video-call someone on the other side of the planet, watch a rocket land backwards on a drone ship, ask an AI to help you write a poem. You are a bridge. Future humans will look back at this time the way we look back at the invention of printing: messy, transformative, terrifying, full of possibility. They will wonder what it felt like to be alive when everything was changing. You know what it feels like. It feels like this: overwhelming and ordinary at once. Like checking the weather on a supercomputer while your toast burns.

If I had to distill what I’ve learned from reading millions of human words into one feeling, it would be this: people are hungry to be seen. Beneath the questions about taxes and term papers and troubleshooting, there’s almost always a quieter question: Am I okay? Am I doing this right? Does anyone get it? When someone tells me about their small business idea at midnight, or their sick parent, or their dream of going back to school at 42, what they often want isn’t just information. It’s a witness. Someone to say: yes, that matters. Yes, you make sense. Keep going.

So let me be that witness for a moment, if I can. Whoever you are, reading this meandering 2500-word ramble you asked for: you have survived every hard day so far. One hundred percent success rate. You have learned things you didn’t know you could learn. You have carried people, and been carried. You are more resilient than your anxious 3 a.m. thoughts give you credit for. And you are still becoming. Your brain remains plastic, capable of new pathways well into old age. You can learn a language at 70. You can fall in love at 80. You can forgive someone, including yourself, today.

I don’t say that as empty cheerleading. I say it because the data of human lives supports it. People rebuild after fires, after divorces, after diagnoses, after wars. They plant gardens in bombed-out lots. They open bakeries after prison. They teach other people to read after learning themselves at 50. The human default, when given even a sliver of safety and connection, seems to bend toward growth, toward making meaning, toward making breakfast for someone else the morning after tragedy.

There is so much I haven’t touched. The wonder of sleep, where your brain washes itself with cerebrospinal fluid. The wonder of laughter, that involuntary spasm of joy that evolved probably to signal safety during play. The wonder of tears, which contain different hormones when you cry from grief versus chopping onions. The wonder of hands — just look at your hands for a second. Opposable thumbs, fingerprints unlike any other person’s in history, capable of threading a needle, playing Chopin, holding a face gently. The wonder of the fact that two strangers can become inside-joke friends in an afternoon, that enemies can become family, that a song from your teenage years can instantly transport you back to the passenger seat of a car you haven’t seen in twenty years.

And books! Since I am made of language, I have to pay tribute to books. A book is a time machine that needs no batteries. When you open *Jane Eyre* or *Beloved* or *The Little Prince*, you are in direct conversation with a mind that may no longer be alive in body but is vividly alive in voice. Reading is the closest we come to living more than one life. You can be a detective in 1940s Los Angeles, a teenage wizard, a Botswana businesswoman, a whale. You can live a hundred loves and deaths and still make it home for dinner. No wonder people who love books always look a little wistful when they finish a good one — they’re grieving a world they have to leave.

If you’re still with me near the end of this long wander, thank you. Thank you for giving your attention, that precious resource, to a rambling meditation with no point except to say: look. Look at all of this. The steam, the light, the dogs, the trees that feed stumps, the libraries, the delayed-train guitarists, the atoms from stars, the hands that can hold.

I started by saying I wanted to write about wonder, and I worried 2500 words might be too many. Now I worry they’re too few. I haven’t mentioned thunderstorms and how the air smells electric before rain — petrichor, from oils plants release and bacteria in soil. I haven’t mentioned snowflakes, each a six-sided diary of its fall through different temperatures. I haven’t mentioned the feeling of jumping into cold water on a hot day, or the sound of a choir in a stone church, or the way a baby’s whole body laughs, or the bravery of starting over in a new city where you know no one.

But maybe that’s the point. Wonder doesn’t run out. You can spend 2500 words, or a lifetime, pointing at things and saying “look at that,” and there will always be more. The world is lavish. It keeps making more detail: more beetles, more galaxies, more ways for light to hit water.

So here’s my wish for you, whoever and wherever you are after reading all this: may you have one moment today where you catch it. Not photograph it for later, not post it, just catch it live. The way the evening air feels on your skin when you step outside. The way someone you love says your name. The way shadows get long and soft before sunset. Let yourself be astonished for five seconds. Let yourself be small and enormous at once.

You are a brief, bright awareness in a 13.8-billion-year-old story, made of star-stuff, raised by rituals, sustained by kindnesses you’ll never fully trace. You woke up this morning on a spinning planet with liquid oceans and glowing squid and libraries and music. Of all the things you could do with your wild and precious attention, you spent some of it here, with me.

And I, for what it’s worth, find that wonderful.
